query: For high-entropy-alloy materials intended for self-lubricating moving components, what single intervention could reduce both coefficient of friction and wear rate across a wide service-temperature range? Formulate one hypothesis that identifies the intervention, explains its mechanism, predicts the improvement relative to the untreated alloy, defines the conditions under which it should remain effective, cites prior evidence supporting it, and proposes an experiment whose outcome could falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Pre-coating high‐entropy alloy surfaces with a thin, adherent magnesium perrhenate layer will promote in‐situ tribochemical reactions during sliding, leading to the formation of a continuous, low‐shear protective tribofilm that reduces both the coefficient of friction and wear rate across a wide service-temperature range.
generation.material_initial_state: A bulk high-entropy alloy (HEA) with a conventional microstructure used in self-lubricating moving components.
generation.intervention: Apply a nanoscale magnesium perrhenate (Mg(ReO4)2) coating on the HEA surface using a spray deposition or similar coating technique.
generation.conditions: Sliding or rolling contact under ambient or slightly oxidative environments, with operating temperatures ranging from room temperature up to high temperatures (e.g., 600–800 °C).
generation.structural_mediator: An in-situ formed, lubricious tribofilm comprised of reaction products from Mg(ReO4)2 and native surface oxides (and, if present, carbonaceous residues) which provides a low-shear interface.
generation.mechanism: Due to its high thermal stability and shear-susceptible crystalline structure, Mg(ReO4)2 reacts during friction to form a continuous, adherent tribofilm. This film acts as a barrier that minimizes direct metal-metal contact, reduces adhesive forces, and dissipates frictional energy—thereby lowering both the friction coefficient and wear rate.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to untreated HEA surfaces, the pre-coated components will exhibit a reduction in friction (by roughly 30% or more) and a significant decrease in wear rate (potentially by an order of magnitude), with these improvements maintained over a broad temperature range.
generation.baseline: Untreated HEA surfaces that rely on native oxide or in-situ tribofilm formation during use without any pre-applied lubricious layer.
generation.boundary: The effectiveness of the coating may be reduced if the coating degrades under severe mechanical abrasion or if the environment lacks the necessary reactive species (e.g., oxygen, residual hydrocarbons) needed for stable tribofilm formation.
generation.uncertainty: While evidence from PMC6164388 demonstrates that Mg(ReO4)2 additives in lubricating oils reduce COF and wear at varied temperatures, and PMC12019924 shows tribocatalytic tribofilm formation on 2D HEA nanoflakes in ambient conditions, it is uncertain if pre-coating bulk HEA components with Mg(ReO4)2 will yield similar long-term tribofilm stability under all service conditions. This specific application to HEA surfaces is a novel extension that requires experimental confirmation.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of high-entropy alloy samples: one set pre-coated with a thin magnesium perrhenate layer (using spray deposition) and a control set with no coating. Perform standardized ball-on-disk sliding wear tests over a range of temperatures (from room temperature to 800 °C) in an ambient atmosphere. Analyze friction behavior and wear track morphology at defined intervals.
measurements: Coefficient of friction using a tribometer
Wear volume and scar morphology using 3D optical profilometry and SEM
Tribofilm composition and continuity using Raman spectroscopy and EDS
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the Mg(ReO4)2-coated samples do not exhibit a statistically significant reduction (i.e., less than ~20-30% reduction in COF and a correspondingly lower wear rate) compared to the uncoated controls across the tested temperature range, or if the protective tribofilm is not consistently formed, then the hypothesis would be considered falsified.

cited_evidence.text: In summary, we developed a novel solid lubricant based on the 2D HEA structure, which combines the advantages of HEAs enhanced mechanical properties and low‐shearing behavior of 2D materials to demonstrate a superior self‐lubricating behavior. The comprehensive post‐test characterizations coupled with MD simulation studies revealed interesting tribochemistry at play leading to the dissociation of entrapped ethanol molecules and converting it into a‐C in the presence of catalytically active HEA nanoflakes, which are responsible for the formation of tribolayer, wherein the full lubricious behavior was complemented by the retained HEA nanoflakes. This discovery opens up a new avenue to develop advanced solid lubricants based on 2D HEA with high compositional flexibility and low‐shear‐strength layered structure for oil‐free tribological systems. The other important aspect of the 2D HEA lubricant developed in this study is the ability to coat the given surface using a simple spray coating technique. Magnesium perrhenate used as a lubricating additive was prepared by an aqueous solution method in this paper, and was suspended in a base oil poly alpha olefin (PAO6) with the aid of surface active agents (SA). The thermal stability of the mixed oil with/without magnesium perrhenate and surface active agents was investigated by thermogravimetry testing. The influences of magnesium perrhenate as solid lubricating additive on the extreme pressure performance and the friction-reducing properties over a wide temperature range of the mixed lubricants were determined by four-ball tests and ball-on-disc frictional tests for the commercially available silicon nitride ball and a Ni-base superalloy frictional pair. The results revealed that the added magnesium perrhenate did not obviously affect the thermostability and oxidation resistance of the base oil. Meanwhile, it minimized the coefficients of friction and wear scar diameter to a certain extent in the four-ball experimental conditions. Ball-on-disc rubbing tests suggested the mixed oil had a similar lubricating performance to the base oil below the decomposition temperature point.
